sections.h2: What is a land contract in Indiana, and how common is it?
sections.html:
A land contract is a financing arrangement in which the seller finances the purchase directly and the buyer pays in installments until the balance is repaid. In most cases the seller keeps the deed until the last payment, so the buyer lives in the house and carries repairs, maintenance and property taxes without holding legal title.

Indiana uses them more than its size suggests. Pew counted 31,431 recorded land contracts from 2005 to 2024, the sixth-most of any state, while Indiana ranked 17th in population in 2024. About 90 percent financed residential property. Recordings peaked at 3,521 in 2010, fell to a low of 612 in 2017 and reached 1,098 in 2024.

The counties with the highest land contract shares of home sales were Jennings at 5.3 percent, Howard at 4.9, Elkhart at 4.3 and Washington at 4.1. Pew also found that corporate entities made up 30 percent of land contract sellers, and in Marion County nearly half of land contracts involved companies.

sections.h2: Does Indiana have one law for land contracts?
sections.html:
No, Indiana has no comprehensive land contract statute. Pew's 2026 fact sheet says the rules are spread across the First Lien Mortgage Lending Act, the Home Loan Practices Act and the 1973 Indiana Supreme Court case Skendzel v. Marshall.

A 2021 National Consumer Law Center summary, which Pew hosts, fills in what those laws do for a land installment contract:

  • A creditor that regularly extends first lien credit, including through land installment contracts, must be licensed by the state.
  • Covered creditors may not engage in unfair or deceptive practices, must give a timely payoff on request and may not charge a prepayment penalty.
  • Creditors that regularly make land installment contracts fall under the Home Loan Practices Act ban on deceptive and misleading acts, IC 24-9-3-7.

Pew adds that Indiana sets no limits on interest rates, fees or contract terms for these deals, and a contract does not have to be publicly recorded. That gap is why two contracts on similar houses can read very differently.

sections.h2: What must an Indiana land contract seller disclose?
sections.html:
A seller under a land contract must tell the buyer about any encumbrance on the property that affects title, and must do it in writing by certified mail with return receipt requested. IC 24-9-3-7(d) names tax liens, foreclosure actions and judgments as examples.

The timing depends on when the encumbrance appears. If it already exists at or before signing, the notice is due no later than signing. If it arises afterward, the notice is due within ten business days after it is created. A seller who misses the deadline commits a prohibited act under the same statute.

The residential disclosure form is a second layer. Indiana Code 32-21-5-1 says the seller-disclosure chapter reaches installment sales contracts, as well as sales, exchanges and lease-purchase deals, for residential real estate with no more than four dwelling units. The owner must complete and sign the form and give it to the buyer before accepting an offer, and an owner is not liable for an error that was outside the owner's actual knowledge, unless the owner was negligent in obtaining or passing on the information.

Transfers by a fiduciary of an estate, trust or guardianship, and transfers by a lender after foreclosure, sit outside that chapter. A seller in one of those roles should not assume the form applies.

sections.h2: Can an Indiana seller keep the buyer's payments after a default?
sections.html:
Not automatically. Indiana courts treat many land contracts like mortgages, so a seller who wants out after a default is often steered toward foreclosure instead of forfeiture. The key case is Skendzel v. Marshall, decided by the Indiana Supreme Court in 1973.

In that case the parties signed a $36,000 contract in December 1958. The buyers had paid $21,000 and still owed $15,000 when they stopped paying after January 1965. The sellers tried to enforce a clause letting them keep every payment and retake the house. The Supreme Court reversed and sent the case back with instructions to foreclose the vendor's lien under the mortgage foreclosure statute.

The court's reasoning has stayed influential:

  • The retained title works like a lien that secures the unpaid balance.
  • Forfeiture is not banned outright, but it should be used "with great caution and only where fairness and justice demand it."
  • Judicial foreclosure, which includes a six-month redemption period, protects the seller's security while preserving the buyer's substantial rights.

Morris v. Weigle (1978) applied the idea. A buyer had paid about 29.7 percent of the price and had not abandoned the farm, so the court rejected the seller's claim to keep $24,722.97 and ordered foreclosure. The decisions describe forfeiture as fitting an abandoning buyer, or a buyer who paid very little, has little equity and stays in possession while the seller covers taxes, insurance and upkeep.

sections.h2: How do contract terms change those protections in practice?
sections.html:
Written terms can narrow the buyer's cushion even when the case law is favorable. Pew found that in Marion County many contracts limit foreclosure to buyers who have paid at least 15 percent to 60 percent of the balance.

A Fair Housing Center of Central Indiana review of about 40 Marion County contracts, as reported by WFYI, found default terms that let sellers file for eviction without notice. A mortgage lender would have to go through foreclosure, which gives the homeowner a chance to pay the debt and keep the house. Some people were reportedly removed without any eviction or foreclosure filing.

WFYI also reported that Indiana lawmakers have considered requiring land contracts to be filed with the county clerk, but that bill never reached the governor. Illinois, by comparison, requires sellers to record within ten business days of the sale. For a seller in Indiana the lack of a filing duty means the file in your own drawer, and the payment history in it, may be the best proof of what happened.

sections.h2: What should you check before selling a house tied to a land contract?
sections.html:
Start by identifying who holds title today and what the contract still requires. Because the seller keeps the deed in most land contracts, ownership of the house and the right to live in it sit with different people until the last payment.

  • The payment record. Total paid and balance owed show how much equity the buyer holds, which matters under Skendzel.
  • Default language. Look for any percentage threshold that limits foreclosure, and for clauses that allow eviction without notice.
  • Liens and judgments. A seller owes the buyer certified mail notice of any encumbrance that affects title.
  • Property taxes. Confirm who has been paying them. A buyer under a recorded contract who pays the taxes may be the one claiming the homestead deduction.
  • Recording. A recorded instrument must be acknowledged by a notarial officer and must state the grantee's mailing address, which must be a street or rural route address under IC 32-21-2-3.

Equity in the house, an unpaid balance and a buyer still living there all affect what a purchaser can do. Gather the contract, the payment history, any default notices and a title report, and take them to an Indiana attorney before signing anything new.

This page is general information, so the contract's effect on a sale is a question for your own lawyer.

faqs.q: Is a land contract legal in Indiana?
faqs.a: Yes. Indiana allows land contracts, though there is no single statute that governs them. The rules come from the First Lien Mortgage Lending Act, the Home Loan Practices Act and case law such as Skendzel v. Marshall.

faqs.q: Do land contracts have to be recorded in Indiana?
faqs.a: No. Pew reports that Indiana contracts do not have to be publicly recorded, which is why the total number in the state is unknown. Lawmakers have considered a filing requirement, but that bill did not reach the governor.

faqs.q: Can a seller evict a land contract buyer in Indiana?
faqs.a: Sometimes, but the route depends on the buyer's equity and the contract terms. Under Skendzel, courts often require foreclosure instead of forfeiture when a buyer has paid a substantial share of the price.

faqs.q: What does a land contract seller have to tell the buyer?
faqs.a: The seller must send written notice by certified mail, return receipt requested, of any encumbrance that affects title. It is due by signing if the encumbrance already exists, or within ten business days if it appears later.

faqs.q: Does the Indiana seller disclosure form apply to land contracts?
faqs.a: Yes, for residential property with no more than four dwelling units. IC 32-21-5-1 covers installment sales contracts, so the owner completes and signs the form before accepting an offer.

faqs.q: What is the difference between forfeiture and foreclosure on a land contract?
faqs.a: Forfeiture lets the seller keep the payments and retake the house. Foreclosure runs through the court, keeps the buyer's equity in play and includes a six-month redemption period as described in Skendzel.
